candidates.inference: Therefore, a low 5-10 us Top-K filter does not by itself establish constant end-to-end sparse-attention latency; the constant-latency claim is at a fixed token budget, not at a fixed K across page sizes.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): With page size 16 and token budget 2048, K=128 pages; with page size 32, K=64 pages for the same token budget, changing Top-K filtering and page metadata cost.
candidates.conditional consequence: If page size changes at fixed K, the token budget and approximate-attention cost change; if K changes at fixed page size, both Top-K and sparse-attention costs change.
candidates.critical_link: The link is the unit conversion between K pages and token budget via page size; the paper's constant-latency statement is conditioned on a given token budget B.
necessary_conditions: page size is fixed or accounted for when comparing K and token budget
K is small enough that sparse-attention cost is dominated by memory savings
sequence length is long enough for fixed K to be a small fraction of the cache
defeaters: page size and K are chosen to match the same token budget
Top-K overhead is negligible relative to attention
sequence length is long so fixed K yields speedup
do_not_infer: Do not infer that Top-K filtering overhead is the whole Quest latency.
Do not infer that K pages equals a fixed token budget independent of page size.
Do not infer that constant approximate-attention latency at fixed token budget means constant end-to-end latency at fixed K.

quotes.text: Given all criticality scores of the pages, Quest chooses Top-K pages to perform approximate self-attention, where K is a preset constant (e.g. 128, 256).
We define the number of tokens in selected pages as the “Token Budget”.
At a given token budget B, the latency of Approximate attention is a constant regardless of the sequence length.

candidates.mechanism: Sparse attention cost scales with selected tokens/pages; K pages times page size equals token budget, so page size and K jointly determine cost. Therefore, a low 5-10 us Top-K filter does not by itself establish constant end-to-end sparse-attention latency; the constant-latency claim is at a fixed token budget, not at a fixed K across page sizes.

candidates.headline: A cheap first-stage page estimate does not guarantee net end-to-end speedup.
candidates.claim: Quest's two-stage design reduces KV-cache memory movement, but the extra criticality-estimation pass and Top-K filtering can dominate at short sequence lengths or small batches, so reported 32K-context speedups do not imply net speedup for all contexts.
candidates.paper_fact: At short sequence length, the memory bandwidth utilization of estimation is smaller than that of FlashInfer, as the total memory load size is not enough to fully utilize GPU memory bandwidth.
candidates.premise: GPU memory-bound kernels need enough work to amortize launch, Top-K, and estimation overhead; at small sizes fixed overheads can dominate.
candidates.inference: Quest's reported 7.03x self-attention and 2.23x end-to-end speedups at 32K do not imply net speedup at short contexts or small batches; the extra estimation pass may not amortize.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): full attention loads 1 MB in 10 us; estimation plus Top-K costs 8 us and sparse attention loads 0.2 MB in 2 us, so net is 10 us, not a speedup; at smaller cache the fixed 8 us dominates.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If sequence length is short or batch is small, then estimation and Top-K overhead can offset memory savings, yielding no net latency gain or a slowdown.
candidates.critical_link: Net benefit threshold: the extra estimation pass must save more full-KV loading than it costs.
necessary_conditions: Long enough context or large enough batch to saturate memory bandwidth
Estimation and Top-K overhead small relative to saved KV loading
Sparse attention kernel supports selected pages efficiently
K and page size chosen so saved bytes exceed extra pass cost
defeaters: Measured net speedup at short contexts
Fused estimation and attention kernel with negligible launch overhead
Large batch that saturates bandwidth even at short context
Paper's own short-context measurements showing no regression
do_not_infer: Do not infer Quest is slower at all short contexts; the paper reports speedups at 32K and the short-context case is an inferred boundary.
Do not infer the authors claim universal end-to-end speedup across all lengths and hardware.
Do not infer accuracy from latency; this candidate is about net speedup only.
Do not infer the extra pass is always wasteful; it may amortize at long context.
author_boundaries: Authors report speedups at 32K sequence length and specific hardware; they do not claim short-context speedup.
Authors' efficiency analysis assumes memory-bound decode and excludes sampling.

quotes.text: At short sequence length, the memory bandwidth utilization of estimation is smaller than that of FlashInfer, as the total memory load size is not enough to fully utilize GPU memory bandwidth.
At sequence length 32K and token budget 2048, Quest boosts inference speed by 1.74× with FP16 weights and 2.23× with 4-bit quantized weight.

candidates.mechanism: GPU memory-bound kernels need enough work to amortize launch, Top-K, and estimation overhead; at small sizes fixed overheads can dominate. Quest's reported 7.03x self-attention and 2.23x end-to-end speedups at 32K do not imply net speedup at short contexts or small batches; the extra estimation pass may not amortize.

candidates.headline: Skipping Quest in the first two layers does not guarantee accuracy preservation on models whose early-layer sparsity differs from LongChat-7B.
candidates.claim: The fixed two-layer exemption is an empirical, model-specific choice; it is not a general accuracy guarantee for other architectures or tasks.
candidates.paper_fact: Due to the low sparsity ratio for the first two layers (as shown in Fig. 3), we only apply Quest and all baselines on later layers to better preserve model accuracy.
candidates.premise: Layer-wise attention sparsity is an empirical property that can vary with model architecture, training data, task, and evaluation metric; a threshold validated on one model/dataset is not a universal guarantee.
candidates.inference: The two-layer skip is a model-specific empirical rule, not a per-layer safety guarantee; on a model with dense attention beyond layer two, the same skip could leave important dense layers sparsified or exempt the wrong layers.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a hypothetical model with dense attention in layers 1-4 would be only partially protected by a two-layer skip.
candidates.conditional consequence: If a target model has dense attention in layer 3 or later, then applying Quest only after layer 2 may lose accuracy unless the exemption threshold is adapted or validated.
candidates.critical_link: The paper's evidence for the threshold is a sparsity measurement on LongChat-7B with PG19 perplexity; it does not establish per-layer safety for other models or tasks.
necessary_conditions: The target model's layer-wise sparsity must match the observed pattern.
The accuracy metric must be sensitive to the exempted layers.
The two-layer threshold must be validated on the target workload.
defeaters: Replicated sparsity pattern across target models.
Later layers remain highly sparse.
Accuracy is unchanged by the fixed skip.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that Quest's page-selection algorithm is invalid.
Do not infer a specific safe layer count for another model.
Do not infer measured accuracy loss from this analysis.
author_boundaries: Authors report a two-layer skip for their evaluated LongChat/Yarn models and call it orthogonal to the selection algorithm; they do not claim a universal layer threshold.
inferred_consequences: A deployment on a different architecture may need an adaptive or validated layer rule.

quotes.text: For the first two layers, the sparsity is below 10%, while for the rest of the layers, the sparsity is larger than 90%, showing great potential for optimization.
Due to the low sparsity ratio for the first two layers (as shown in Fig. 3), we only apply Quest and all baselines on later layers to better preserve model accuracy.
Note that whether to skip the first two layers or not is orthogonal to the KV cache selection algorithm.

The two-layer skip is a model-specific empirical rule, not a per-layer safety guarantee; on a model with dense attention beyond layer two, the same skip could leave important dense layers sparsified or exempt the wrong layers.

candidates.headline: The observed layer-wise sparsity does not guarantee that the first two layers are the only dense layers across tasks or sequence lengths.
candidates.claim: The layer exception is based on a sparsity measurement on LongChat-7B with a PG19 perplexity criterion; it is not a per-layer guarantee for other tasks, metrics, or context lengths.
candidates.paper_fact: We measure the sparsity by eliminating KV cache tokens while making sure the perplexity on PG19 increases less than 0.01.
candidates.premise: Sparsity depends on model, task, metric, and sequence length; a single measurement under one criterion does not guarantee the same layer-wise pattern elsewhere.
candidates.inference: The fixed two-layer skip may be misaligned for tasks or models with different layer-wise sparsity; the origin and stability of the observed regularity are not established.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a task whose answer requires attention in layer 3 could be harmed if layer 3 is sparsified under a two-layer rule.
candidates.conditional consequence: If a task requires dense attention in later layers or if early layers become sparse, then the fixed two-layer rule may be suboptimal or accuracy-degrading unless revalidated.
candidates.critical_link: The evidence is a sparsity profile on LongChat-7B using PG19 perplexity increase below 0.01; it does not establish that the first two layers are universally the only dense layers.
necessary_conditions: Same model and task distribution.
Same sparsity criterion, such as PG19 perplexity increase below 0.01.
Same accuracy target.
Layer sparsity measured under the relevant context length.
defeaters: Sparsity pattern replicated across tasks and models.
Early layers remain dense.
Later layers remain highly sparse.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that all later layers are always sparse.
Do not infer exact sparsity ratios for other models.
Do not infer that the first two layers are universally dense.
author_boundaries: Authors measure sparsity on LongChat-7B with PG19 perplexity and apply the skip in their evaluated models; they do not claim the pattern is universal.
inferred_consequences: A fixed two-layer rule may be misaligned for tasks or models with different layer-wise sparsity.

candidates.headline: Retaining the full KV cache does not imply or guarantee reduced KV-cache memory capacity.
candidates.claim: Quest's full-cache retention and per-query page selection reduce memory movement during decode, but they do not reduce the KV-cache storage footprint; capacity-bound deployments gain no capacity from Quest alone.
candidates.paper_fact: Quest does not discard KV cache but instead uses a query-aware approach to identify critical tokens.
candidates.premise: KV-cache size scales with sequence length and model dimensions; retaining all entries keeps the storage footprint; selecting pages changes bytes loaded per attention step, not bytes allocated.
candidates.inference: Therefore Quest's reported speedup is a bandwidth/memory-movement benefit, not a capacity benefit, and it cannot by itself increase the maximum context length under a fixed memory budget.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a 32K-token Llama-7B KV cache is about 16GB; selecting 2K tokens per query still requires storing the full 16GB cache.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a deployment is capacity-bound, then Quest alone will not fit longer contexts; additional eviction, quantization, or offloading is needed.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is that full retention and per-query selection alter what is loaded for attention, not what is stored in the KV cache.
necessary_conditions: Full KV cache is stored for all tokens
Selection only chooses pages to load for attention
Metadata min/max per page is stored
Decode is bandwidth-bound rather than capacity-bound
defeaters: Implementation also evicts or compresses KV cache
Quest is combined with quantization or offloading that reduces capacity
Workload is compute-bound rather than bandwidth-bound
do_not_infer: Quest reduces KV-cache memory footprint
Quest alone enables longer context under fixed GPU memory
Quest eliminates the need for eviction or quantization

quotes.text: Quest does not discard KV cache but instead uses a query-aware approach to identify critical tokens.
Instead of loading the whole KV cache, Quest only needs to load a fraction of the data, which leverages query-aware sparsity.
During criticality estimation, Quest will load maximal and minimal vectors of each page, which is approximately 2M ∗L/S bytes.

author_boundaries: Authors claim speedup from reduced memory movement, not reduced KV-cache allocation; they do not claim capacity savings.
inferred_consequences: Capacity-bound deployments need additional memory reduction; Quest alone cannot increase max context under fixed memory.
candidates.mechanism: KV-cache size scales with sequence length and model dimensions; retaining all entries keeps the storage footprint; selecting pages changes bytes loaded per attention step, not bytes allocated. Therefore Quest's reported speedup is a bandwidth/memory-movement benefit, not a capacity benefit, and it cannot by itself increase the maximum context length under a fixed memory budget.
